paragraphs.title: Tyre’s Joy over Jerusalem’s Destruction and Its Coming Punishment

easy.explanation: Tyre said of Jerusalem, “Aha, she is broken that was the gates of the people.”
easy.q: Over the destruction of which city did Tyre rejoice?

easy.explanation: The LORD said, “I will cause many nations to come up against thee.”
easy.q: What did the LORD say He would bring against Tyre?

answers: They would be slain by the sword
easy.explanation: The prophecy says, “her daughters which are in the field shall be slain by the sword.”
easy.q: What would happen to Tyre’s daughters in the field?

answers: Because Tyre rejoiced over Jerusalem’s destruction
Because Tyre had asked for peace
medium.explanation: Tyre rejoiced at Jerusalem’s fall and expected to benefit from it, but judgment was announced against Tyre.
medium.q: Why would the LORD bring many nations against Tyre?

medium.explanation: The image describes Tyre as exposed, barren, and stripped of its former city life.
medium.q: What does “the top of a rock” suggest about Tyre’s future condition?

answers: They will come to restore it
They will come to trade with it
They will come to destroy it
medium.explanation: The nations will destroy Tyre’s walls and make it a spoil.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the coming nations and Tyre’s fate?

answers: Tyre expected to profit from Jerusalem’s ruin, but Tyre itself would be ruined
Tyre expected peace, but received trade
Tyre expected to be rebuilt, but Jerusalem was rebuilt
challenge.explanation: Tyre hoped to take Jerusalem’s place, but the LORD declared that destruction would come upon Tyre.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears between Tyre’s expectation and the LORD’s announcement?

answers: It will become a royal center
It will become an open and desolate place
It will remain a fortified city
challenge.explanation: A place for spreading nets is exposed and empty rather than a populated city.
challenge.q: What does the image of a place where nets are spread reveal about Tyre’s future?

challenge.explanation: The prophecy repeatedly emphasizes, “I the LORD have spoken it.”
challenge.q: What gives the prophecy its final authority?

paragraphs.title: The Babylonian Siege and the Destruction of the City

easy.explanation: The LORD said He would bring Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon against Tyre.
easy.q: Who would lead the army coming against Tyre?

easy.explanation: The verse says that he would come “from the north.”
easy.q: From which direction would Nebuchadrezzar come?

answers: They would cease and be heard no more
easy.explanation: The LORD said, “I will cause the noise of thy songs to cease.”
easy.q: What would happen to Tyre’s songs and the sound of its harps?

answers: A military structure used against the city
medium.explanation: The army would build a fort and a mount as part of its attack on Tyre.
medium.q: What is a “fort” in the description of the siege?

answers: Siege, breaching the walls, destruction, and plunder
medium.explanation: The army would besiege the city, break its defenses, kill its people, destroy its buildings, and take its wealth.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the army’s actions against Tyre?

answers: They would be stored in the palace
They would be carried to Jerusalem
They would be placed in the midst of the water
medium.explanation: The prophecy says they would lay Tyre’s stones, timber, and dust “in the midst of the water.”
medium.q: What would happen to Tyre’s stones, timber, and dust after the destruction?

challenge.explanation: The many horses, horsemen, and chariots portray a large and powerful invading army.
challenge.q: What do the horses, chariots, horsemen, and dust emphasize about the army?

answers: Tyre loses its people, wealth, and buildings
Tyre becomes a center of music
challenge.explanation: The army kills the people, plunders the riches, destroys the walls and houses, and casts the building materials into the water.
challenge.q: What is the overall result of the army’s actions in this passage?

answers: The city becomes quiet because of a celebration
The city moves to another place
The city’s life and activity come to an end
challenge.explanation: The silencing of the songs represents the end of Tyre’s public life after its destruction.
challenge.q: What does the change from “the noise of thy songs” to “no more heard” signify?

paragraphs.title: The Nations Tremble at Tyre’s Fall

answers: The isles and peoples across the sea
easy.explanation: The passage says that the isles would shake and the isles in the sea would be troubled.
easy.q: Who would tremble at the fall of Tyre?

answers: Lay away their robes and remove their splendid garments
easy.explanation: They would lay away their robes, put off their broidered garments, and sit upon the ground.
easy.q: What would the princes of the sea do?

answers: The building of a new city
easy.explanation: They would lament and ask, “How art thou destroyed?”
easy.q: For what would the nations take up a lamentation?

medium.explanation: A lamentation is an expression of grief over loss or destruction.
medium.q: What is a “lamentation” in this passage?

answers: Tyre had been a powerful and feared maritime city
Tyre had been a small inland village
Tyre had been built in the desert
medium.explanation: Tyre was renowned, strong in the sea, and a source of terror to those who lived around it.
medium.q: Why would Tyre’s fall affect the isles and peoples across the sea?

medium.explanation: These actions express grief, fear, and humiliation in response to Tyre’s fall.
medium.q: What do the princes’ removal of their garments and sitting on the ground show?

answers: It is limited to Tyre itself
It spreads to nations and isles across the sea
challenge.explanation: The passage describes trembling and mourning among the princes of the sea and the isles.
challenge.q: What is the scope of the response to Tyre’s fall?

answers: From a strong and renowned city to a destroyed city
From a poor city to a wealthy city
From an inland city to a desert city
challenge.explanation: The lament recalls Tyre’s former strength and fame while describing its destruction.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between Tyre’s former condition and its condition after the fall?

answers: That its fall was astonishing because of its former strength
challenge.explanation: The question emphasizes the shocking contrast between Tyre’s former greatness and its ruin.
challenge.q: What does the question “How art thou destroyed?” imply?

paragraphs.title: Tyre’s Descent into Ruin and Disappearance

easy.explanation: The LORD says that the deep would come up and great waters would cover Tyre.
easy.q: What would cover Tyre in the prophecy?

answers: To the top of a mountain
To the land of the living
To the pit and the low parts of the earth
easy.explanation: Tyre is described as being brought down with those who descend into the pit.
easy.q: Where would Tyre be brought down?

answers: It would disappear and never be found again
It would become the capital of the nations
easy.explanation: The LORD says, “though thou be sought for, yet shalt thou never be found again.”
easy.q: What would Tyre’s final condition be?

medium.explanation: The land of the living refers to the realm of life, in contrast with the low and desolate places of the dead.
medium.q: What does “the land of the living” represent in contrast with the pit?

answers: It becomes a great trading city
It becomes a terror and is no more
It comes under the rule of the sea princes
medium.explanation: The LORD says, “I will make thee a terror, and thou shalt be no more.”
medium.q: How is Tyre’s removal from the inhabited world described?

answers: Both describe its sinking and destruction
medium.explanation: Both images portray Tyre as removed from the inhabited world and brought into ruin.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the covering waters and Tyre’s descent to the pit?

answers: It will no longer be inhabited
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes that Tyre will cease to be a dwelling place for people.
challenge.q: What does “that thou be not inhabited” emphasize about Tyre’s future?

answers: Life and the realm of death and desolation
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the inhabited land of the living with the low, desolate places associated with the dead.
challenge.q: What conceptual contrast appears between “the land of the living” and the pit?

answers: The promise that it will soon be found
The statement that it will never be found again
The promise that it will be rebuilt
challenge.explanation: The words “never be found again” express the complete and permanent nature of Tyre’s disappearance.
